tier_reason: The benchmark page compares plf::list directly with std::list. It states MinGW GCC 9.2 x64, -O2 -march=native and an Intel Xeon E3-1241 (Haswell). The benchmark code is public as the 'plf benchmark suite' zip linked from the colony page downloads section (https://plflib.org/plf_benchmark_suite_08-07-2026.zip, HTTP 200).

corrections.claimed_speedup: On the benchmark page: insertion 333% faster on average (raw tests across char/int/double/small-struct/large-struct); sort 77% faster than std::list's internal sort (average of all tests); reverse 70% faster; remove/remove_if 91% faster; unique 63% faster; clear() 1,147,900% faster on average for trivially-destructible small structs (811% for non-trivially-destructible); destruction 6,350% faster (1,248% for non-trivially-destructible); about 25% faster than std::list in ordered low- and high-modification 'real-world' scenario tests. For erasure the page gives no percentage, only 'best erasure performance until very large amounts of memory are involved'.
corrections.workload: Raw insertion/erasure/iteration tests across char, int, double, small struct and large struct (490-byte) element types; list-specific tests (sort, reverse, remove/remove_if, unique, clear, destruction) and ordered 'real-world' modification scenarios using small structs only; project's own plf benchmark suite
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark, though code, compiler, flags and CPU are all published. Only libstdc++ (MinGW GCC 9.2) is tested, not libc++ or MSVC STL. The extreme clear/destruction figures apply to trivially-destructible types; for non-trivially-destructible types they drop to 811%/1,248%. The README's 57% erasure / 17% iteration / 20-24% overall / 293% insertion figures (GCC 8.1) do not appear on this benchmark page.

notes: The tier stays A, but the claim mixed README figures (57% erasure, 17% iteration, 20-24% overall) with benchmark-page figures. It also labelled trivially-destructible-only clear/destruction numbers as averages across types, so claimed_speedup was rewritten to match the page. Metadata checks out: Zlib, 176 stars, last commit 2026-09-19, not a fork.

tier_reason: N2271 Appendix item 20 is a first-party performance table from EA, not peer-reviewed and not an independent suite. It shows the vector<uint64> ratios exactly as claimed (push_back 1.63/2.18/1.02/1.59; Linux operator[] 1.29; sort 0.92). It is not A: the paper's benchmark source is only 'distributed with this document' and not linked, and the CPU is given only by family (Pentium 4, 64-bit PowerPC, G5).

corrections.caveats: Data is from a 2007 WG21 paper, a first-party EA submission and not peer-reviewed or independent. Hardware (Pentium 4, G5 and console PowerPC) and compilers (GCC 4.0/4.1, VC7/8) are about two decades old. On libstdc++ the push_back gain is only 1.02x; the larger wins are against compiler-supplied MSVC STL (VC8) and the console VC7 STL. On Linux/libstdc++, sort (0.92x) was slower. The current repo ships benchmark/source/BenchmarkVector.cpp, but no recent published numbers confirm these ratios.

notes: All ratios were verified in the Appendix 20 table (columns: A Windows VC8, B Console VC7, C Linux GCC 4.1/libstdc++, D Mac GCC 4.0/libstdc++). Tier lowered from B to C because a first-party committee paper is not peer review. last_commit corrected to the default-branch commit date; 2025-11-15 was pushed_at from another branch. Still active; BSD-3-Clause, 9,367 stars.

tier_reason: The README shows first-party Google Benchmark output against std::vector on an i7-4720HQ with VS2017. The repo contains no benchmark code (only fast_vector.h, README.md and LICENSE) and states no optimization flags, so it is not A.

corrections.caveats: Only tested against MSVC STL on one Windows machine; no libstdc++ or libc++ numbers. Build configuration and flags are not stated, and the benchmark source is not in the repo. For non-trivial types, reserve+push_back is a wash (std 88,303ns vs fast_vector 88,671ns) and push_back+pop_back is only ~1.06x (101,814 vs 96,396ns). No commits since 2019.

notes: All claimed timings match the README exactly, and the derived ratios are correct. last_commit corrected to the default-branch commit date (the 2019-06-21 date was pushed_at). MIT, 21 stars, not archived.

tier_reason: docs/tiered_vector.md (current and 2022/2023 revisions) has only the qualitative 'several order of magnitudes faster than std::deque' claim. It gives no timings, sizes, compiler or CPU. benchs/bench_tiered_vector.cpp compares std::vector, std::deque and tiered_vector, but no output from it is published anywhere found.
notes: No numbers for tiered_vector vs std::deque, and the repo has 111 stars (under 1k, not widely referenced), so the rejection is for this record's claim only. Other seq components do have first-party chart benchmarks against std containers: docs/sorted_benchmark.md (seq::flat_set/radix_set vs std::set, i7-10850H, flags unstated). Those could be a separate associative-container record. last_commit corrected to the default-branch (main) commit; 2026-09-21 was pushed_at from another branch.

tier_reason: performance/main.cpp is public benchmark code with a sample-output comment labelled 'g++-9 -O3' comparing std::deque, std::vector and veque. No CPU model is stated, so it is not A.

corrections.caveats: First-party sample output in a source comment, with no CPU model. The stdlib vendor is not named (presumably libstdc++ via g++-9). The sample is labelled g++-9, while current code targets C++20/23, so it may be stale. veque is slower than std::deque on back growth (552,027 vs 342,218us) and front growth (30,739 vs 16,386us), and roughly equal to std::vector on iteration (207,987 vs 203,040us). The 217x front-growth ratio is an algorithmic worst case for std::vector.

notes: All totals and per-test numbers match the source comment, and the derived ratios (~4.1x, ~1.4x, ~217x) are correct. The workload (7 tests, each run 3 times per container, 2M-element iteration) matches main(). BSL-1.0, 128 stars, last commit 2026-09-15.
